storyboard.claim: Jack lists four specific reasons he genuinely likes Auggie — starting with you just get used to his face.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack talking in the classroom beside Auggie, both relaxed — the friendship is real.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Jack's internal shift made explicit: obligation has become affection.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two boys together in the classroom shows this is a functioning friendship, not a managed duty.

callout.text: Auggie covers for Jack — loyalty, not obligation

storyboard.claim: Auggie is smart, lets Jack copy his homework, and even lies to the teacher to cover for them — a genuine bro move.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack holding Auggie's notes with a smirk — the academic collusion that seals the friendship.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the list of reasons: this is intimacy and loyalty, not duty.
storyboard.addedInformation: The hold of the notes makes the cheating literal and visible without any spoken words.

storyboard.claim: If Jack could line up every fifth-grade boy and choose anyone, he would genuinely choose Auggie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack pointing — making an active, decisive choice — in the classroom.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The fourth and most poignant reason: not habit, not duty — a free choice.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pointing action makes the choosing physical; the happy face confirms it is not reluctant.

storyboard.claim: Jack's arc perfectly illustrates the evolution from a mandate to a free choice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow diagram: Obligation → Genuine choice — the spine of Jack's transformation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarises the four-reason list as a single arc.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram gives the arc a visual label the narration only names abstractly.

storyboard.claim: Forcing 10-year-olds to be a welcoming committee is deeply manipulative.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman pointing — the principal directing children into a role they did not choose.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pushback: the same arc that looks like growth looks like manipulation from another angle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk (official smile that does not reach the eyes) signals the problem with the method without needing words.

storyboard.claim: A 10-year-old lacks the emotional maturity, life experience, and prefrontal cortex to process profound facial deformity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack in the classroom, worried and thinking — the image of developmental unreadiness.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the charge of manipulation in child psychology.
storyboard.addedInformation: The thinking-face shows internal struggle; worried rather than neutral conveys the real cognitive burden.

storyboard.claim: Tushman thrusts children into a situation demanding perfect ambassadors of empathy — setting them up to fail.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman pointing at Jack in the classroom: the adult assigning an impossible role to a child.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the critique: not just manipulative in intent but structurally unfair.
storyboard.addedInformation: Two cast members (authority figure + child) make the power imbalance visible without words.

storyboard.claim: What Tushman is really doing is installing moral training wheels.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Choose Kind sign behind Tushman — the slogan is the training wheel itself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The counter-argument begins: gives Tushman's method a structural name.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book's own icon (Choose Kind) names the system Tushman is building.

storyboard.claim: Empathy doesn't bloom magically — sometimes it must be modeled and structured, like scaffolding on a building.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman talking calmly in the classroom — the architect explaining his plan.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Develops the 'training wheels' metaphor with the scaffolding analogy.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the scaffolding is a spoken metaphor; we stage the explainer, not the building.

storyboard.claim: Without Tushman's forced interaction, Jack would never have sat down with Auggie — fear of judgment would have won.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack alone in the cafeteria, worried — the counterfactual: no Tushman, no connection.
storyboard.onScreenText: Jack would never sit with August
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The scaffolding thesis proven: only the structured space produced the friendship.
storyboard.addedInformation: Subjunctive phrasing (would never) signals a hypothetical, not a current fact.

storyboard.claim: The arrangement creates a sanctioned adult-approved space but places an incredibly unfair burden on Jack.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack slumping with a worried face — the weight of the role he never asked for.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concedes the counter-argument a point: the scaffolding has a cost.
storyboard.addedInformation: Slump + worried reads as someone weighed down — the emotional tax of the assignment is visible.

storyboard.claim: Asking a child to do the emotional heavy lifting of an adult is precisely the nature of the moral test.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack thinking and worried in the classroom — the child running the adult experiment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The burden is not a flaw in the design — it IS the design.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the test is abstract; we show the person taking it rather than the test itself.

storyboard.claim: The adults only set up the laboratory — the kids are the ones who run the experiment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: Adults set up lab → Kids run experiment — the division of moral labour.
storyboard.onScreenText: Adults set up lab → Kids run experiment
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the tension: the adult sets conditions, the child determines outcomes.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram makes visible the structural role split the narration names.

storyboard.claim: Jack chooses to stay in the room — he builds the building himself — right up until the scaffolding falls.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Auggie sitting together in the cafeteria, Jack happy — genuine choice visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Jack passes the test — temporarily. The 'right up until' is the hinge.
storyboard.addedInformation: The happy expression shows the choice is real, not coerced, before the betrayal arrives.

storyboard.claim: Jack doesn't stay in the room forever — the test completely breaks him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack alone, sad and slumping — the collapse after the betrayal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pivot: from the hopeful friendship to its most agonising failure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chapter title as callout signals a new section; the staging shows the emotional register.

storyboard.claim: Weeks after Halloween, Jack sits in the cafeteria with Summer, totally baffled.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Summer sitting in the cafeteria, Jack worried — the aftermath the viewer needs to see.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Scene-setting: enters the aftermath of the betrayal before it is explained.
storyboard.addedInformation: Summer's presence establishes the specific social configuration that triggers the revelation.

storyboard.claim: Ever since Halloween, August has been icing Jack out — barely speaking, avoiding eye contact.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie angry and turned away while Jack stands nearby — the cold shoulder made visual.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows Auggie's reaction to a wound the viewer does not yet know about.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie first (angry) makes clear who is doing the icing and why — even before the cause is explained.

storyboard.claim: Jack has absolutely no idea why August is avoiding him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack alone in the cafeteria, worried and thinking — completely in the dark.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Jack's ignorance at this point is the dramatic engine — we know he will be devastated.
storyboard.addedInformation: The solo frame underscores his isolation after the break in the friendship.

storyboard.claim: Jack begs Summer for a hint; sworn to secrecy but pitying him, she gives him one devastating clue.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Summer talking to a worried Jack in the cafeteria — the moment of the clue being delivered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summer becomes the messenger who triggers Jack's recollection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Summer first (the one with the information) signals who holds the power in this exchange.

storyboard.claim: Two words — 'Bleeding Scream' — and the bottom drops out of Jack's entire world.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mask icon (the Halloween costume mask) beside Jack afraid and collapsed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The clue lands: two words produce total devastation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask icon reads as 'a false face / someone hidden behind a costume' — exactly the Halloween costume that overheard everything.

storyboard.claim: Jack's brain races back to Halloween morning — standing in homeroom surrounded by Julian and the popular kids.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Julian together in the classroom, Julian smirking — the scene of the original betrayal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The clue triggers memory: we cut back to the event itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian smirking beside Jack places the social pressure that produced the betrayal.

storyboard.claim: They were saying awful things about August — and Jack chimed in.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Julian talking in the classroom, both smirking — Jack joining the cruelty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the flashback: Jack is not just present, he participates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Jack's smirk (matching Julian's) shows he crossed into complicity, not just silence.

storyboard.claim: Jack said he would kill himself if he looked like August, and told Julian he was only pretending to be friends.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack talking to Julian in the classroom — the exact words that will destroy Auggie.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The worst of the betrayal: Jack denies the friendship to Julian's face.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style signals these are the words the book condemns — the rejected claim.

storyboard.claim: Jack remembers a kid in a Bleeding Scream costume sitting at a nearby desk — it was August, in costume, overhearing everything.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie sitting alone behind the astronautHelmet icon — the costume as August's disguise, the thing that hid him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hinge of the flashback: the figure that was there the whole time.
storyboard.addedInformation: AstronautHelmet instead of mask prevents viewer from thinking Jack wore it; helmet = August's costume/hiding.

callout.text: August was there. He heard it all.

storyboard.claim: Jack realises with sickening clarity that August overheard every single word.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone, sad and slumped in the classroom — the weight of what he heard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The realisation completes: the costume was Auggie; the words were heard.
storyboard.addedInformation: The slump after the sad face conveys devastation, not just sorrow.

storyboard.claim: This betrayal lands harder than anything Julian could dish out — August is used to cruelty; it is his baseline.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie walking the corridor alone, neutral — baseline resilience, already armoured.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why Julian's cruelty does not wound as deeply — it is expected.
storyboard.addedInformation: The neutral walking Auggie in the hallway shows someone who has learned to absorb routine hostility.

callout.text: Auggie has armour for Julian already

storyboard.claim: The stares, the whispers, the older kids making monster noises — all a known entity. He has armour for Julian.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian smirking beside Auggie in the hallway — the known threat Auggie has already survived.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the contrast concrete: Julian = familiar cruelty, armoured against.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian first (the threat) and Auggie second (still upright) shows the armour is real.

storyboard.claim: But Jack was his safe harbour — the one who chose him when he didn't have to.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Auggie sitting together in the cafeteria beside the shield icon — the protection Jack represented.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the contrast: Julian = known enemy; Jack = supposed safe zone.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shield reads as protection — the viewer sees what Jack meant to Auggie before the betrayal is named.

storyboard.claim: To find out that safety was an illusion — that Jack was wearing a mask of friendship while stabbing him in the back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack with a smirk (not genuine warmth) beside the mask icon — the fake friend exposed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the wound: the safe harbour was performed, not real.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk rather than happy shows the face behind the face — the viewer reads charm concealing cruelty.

callout.text: THAT DOESNT JUST HURT AUGUSTS FEELINGS

storyboard.claim: It doesn't just hurt August's feelings — it shatters his entire framework of trust.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone, sad and slumped — the structural collapse, not just pain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Stakes the wound properly: existential, not emotional.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: 'framework' is abstract; slump conveys a complete internal collapse that the word only names.

storyboard.claim: On the very first day of school Jack actively chose a table as far from August as possible.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack walking away from Auggie in the cafeteria — the original avoidance made physical.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The second detail: the betrayal goes back to day one, not just Halloween.
storyboard.addedInformation: The walk action with Jack heading away from Auggie shows the direction of the choice.

storyboard.claim: Jack sat with strangers just to talk baseball — a profound moral failure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack sitting comfortably at the cafeteria table, smirking — choosing comfort over loyalty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the cost of day-one avoidance plainly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk on Jack at the comfortable table: the viewer reads self-satisfaction — comfort chosen over conscience.

storyboard.claim: When the pressure was on — claim his friendship publicly in front of peers — Jack folded.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack afraid beside Julian in the hallway — the moment social pressure wins.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pattern confirmed: day one and Halloween both show the same failure of nerve.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian present makes the social threat concrete; Jack's afraid face shows he chose fear over loyalty.

storyboard.claim: He chose his own comfort over his loyalty to a vulnerable kid — acting like a massive hypocrite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack smirking, comfortable, alone in the classroom — self-interest as a default.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the underlying motive: not cruelty but cowardly comfort.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk signals the hypocrisy the narration names — the self-satisfied face of someone who took the easy path.

storyboard.claim: Enjoying August's humour and copying his homework in private — throwing him to the wolves in public.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack smirking comfortably beside Auggie in the hallway — taking in private, abandoning in public.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The double standard made explicit: warmth in private, exposure in public.
storyboard.addedInformation: Both on screen shows the private friendship that Jack enjoyed before discarding publicly.

storyboard.claim: Hold on — we have to defend Jack. The indictment judges a 10-year-old with the moral absolutism of an adult.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack worried and thinking alone in the classroom — the child seen through the child's eyes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The defence opens: changes the frame from verdict to context.
storyboard.addedInformation: The thinking worried child: the viewer recalibrates who is actually on screen.

storyboard.claim: He is a 10-year-old in middle school — an evolutionary battleground.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack alone and afraid in the classroom — the child, not the hypocrite.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Restates the subject: the unit of analysis is a child, not a moral agent.
storyboard.addedInformation: The afraid expression with no antagonist present shows the ambient fear of middle school itself.

storyboard.claim: Step out of line and the apex predators like Julian destroy you socially — it is herd mentality at its most primal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian smirking and pointing in the hallway — the threat that shapes every choice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the specific ecological force that made Jack's cowardice rational.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian alone and pointing: the viewer reads social dominance and threat, confirming the ecology.

storyboard.claim: Jack is terrified of social suicide — the popular kids hold the keys to a comfortable existence for the next 3 years.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack afraid beside a smirking Julian in the hallway — the fear and the source of it in one frame.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the terror in specific consequences: 3 years of social comfort or misery.
storyboard.addedInformation: Jack (afraid) and Julian (smirk) together: the power dynamic that produced the betrayal is visible.

storyboard.claim: Is it cowardly? Yes. But it is intensely understandably human — you cannot expect a 10-year-old to be a martyr for inclusion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack sad and slumping in the classroom — neither villain nor hero, just a child.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict of the defence: guilty but comprehensible.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sad rather than neutral or smirk: the viewer reads remorse or exhaustion — the human cost of his choices.
